top.text:
Irving Morrow, a relatively unknown residential architect, designed the overall shape of the bridge towers, the lighting scheme, and Art Deco elements, such as the tower decorations, streetlights, railing, and walkways. The famous International Orange color was Morrow's personal selection, winning out over other possibilities, including the US Navy's suggestion that it be painted with black and yellow stripes to ensure visibility by passing ships.
Senior engineer Charles Alton Ellis, collaborating remotely with Moisseiff, was the principal engineer of the project. Moisseiff produced the basic structural design, introducing his "deflection theory" by which a thin, flexible roadway would flex in the wind, greatly reducing stress by transmitting forces via suspension cables to the bridge towers. Although the Golden Gate Bridge design has proved sound, a later Moisseiff design, the original Tacoma Narrows Bridge, collapsed in a strong windstorm soon after it was completed, because of an unexpected aeroelastic flutter. Ellis was also tasked with designing a "bridge within a bridge" in the southern abutment, to avoid the need to demolish Fort Point, a pre–Civil War masonry fortification viewed, even then, as worthy of historic preservation. He penned a graceful steel arch spanning the fort and carrying the roadway to the bridge's southern anchorage.

The first rocket ship was created by Robert A. Heinlein, who wrote the novel *Rocket Ship Galileo*, published in 1947. This novel features three teenagers on a pioneering flight to the Moon and was the first in the Heinlein juveniles series.[1][2]

While rockets as a technology have ancient roots, with the Chinese inventing the first rockets during the Song Dynasty, the modern concept of a rocket ship as a vehicle for space travel was pioneered by Robert A. Heinlein in his 1947 novel.[3][4]

The sources describe the Revolution as a period of political and societal change that began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799. The Revolution overthrew the monarchy, established a republic, and experienced violent periods of political turmoil. Its ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, and its values remain central to modern French political discourse.

The fundamental principles of electricity generation were discovered in the 1820s and early 1830s by British scientist Michael Faraday. His method, still used today, is for electricity to be generated by the movement of a loop of wire, or Faraday disc, between the poles of a magnet. Central power stations became economically practical with the development of alternating current (AC) power transmission, using power transformers to transmit power at high voltage and with low loss.
Commercial electricity production started with the coupling of the dynamo to the hydraulic turbine. The mechanical production of electric power began the Second Industrial Revolution and made possible several inventions using electricity, with the major contributors being Thomas Alva Edison and Nikola Tesla. Previously the only way to produce electricity was by chemical reactions or using battery cells, and the only practical use of electricity was for the telegraph.

query: How does 3D printing work?
answer:
3D printing works by converting a virtual 3D model into a physical object, typically by building up successive layers on top of each other. The process follows instructions from a file that provides the steps to print a segment by segment until the object is complete.

A typical 3D printer heats up a filament of plastic and feeds it from a spool; as the plastic cools, it builds the model from the base up. Some printers also use resin, powder, or paper, and there are medical applications that build prosthetics. Larger printers can even use concrete for building.

top.text:
3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, is the construction of a three-dimensional object from a CAD model or a digital 3D model. It can be done in a variety of processes in which material is deposited, joined or solidified under computer control, with the material being added together (e.g. plastics, liquids, or powder grains being fused), typically layer by layer.
In the 1980s, 3D printing techniques were considered suitable only for the production of functional or aesthetic prototypes, and a more appropriate term for it at the time was rapid prototyping. As of 2019, the precision, repeatability, and material range of 3D printing have increased to the point that some 3D printing processes are considered viable as an industrial-production technology; in this context, the term additive manufacturing can be used synonymously with 3D printing. One of the key advantages of 3D printing is the ability to produce very complex shapes or geometries that would be otherwise infeasible to construct by hand, including hollow parts or parts with internal truss structures to reduce weight while creating less material waste. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material, is the most common 3D printing process in use As of 2020.

query: Why are people saying WiFi and radio waves are harmful? What is the evidence?
answer: People say WiFi and radio waves are harmful because they fear that the radio waves emitted by WiFi devices could damage human health, even though official messages claim there is no real danger. The evidence comes from a large body of research, both epidemiological and experimental, in non-human animals and in humans, the majority of which shows no definite causative relationship between exposure to mobile phones and harmful biological effects in humans. A comparison with cell phones indicates that WiFi is a fraction of the energy of a cell phone, and a child on a mobile phone receives up to 50% of guideline levels. There is also a concern that a higher gain antenna could be more troublesome for health, but as long as such official messages have been the same for decades concerning things like tobacco or radioactivity, many people have fears about the possibility.

query: How does an oven work?
answer:
An oven works by exposing materials to a hot environment in a controlled way.

A modern electric or gas oven heats the chamber using a heating element, and a fan circulates hot air around the food[1][3]. A microwave oven works differently: it uses a magnetron to emit microwaves that bounce around the oven, heating water molecules and other molecules in the food[2]. A masonry oven works by soaking up heat like a battery, then radiating that heat back into the food through hot dense bricks, and sealing in steam[4].

So ovens can be heated by hot air, microwaves, or radiant heat from heated walls.

query: What's the difference between a crocodile and an alligator?
answer: Crocodiles and alligators differ in several ways, including their snout shape, teeth visibility, salt gland function, and temperament. Crocodiles have long, narrow V-shaped snouts, while alligators have wider, shovel-like U-shaped snouts. When a crocodile closes its mouth, some teeth are still visible; when an alligator closes its mouth, all teeth are hidden. Crocodiles possess functional salt glands that excrete salt, whereas most alligators and caimans have lost this ability, restricting them to freshwater habitats. Additionally, crocodiles are generally considered more aggressive than alligators.

While there are rules of thumb for distinguishing alligators from crocodiles, all of them admit exceptions. Such general rules include:
Exposed vs. interdigitated teeth: The easiest way to distinguish crocodiles from alligators is by looking at their jaw line. The teeth on the lower jaw of an alligator fit into sockets in the upper jaw, leaving only the upper teeth visible when the mouth is closed. The teeth on the lower jaw of a crocodile fit into grooves on the outside of the top jaw, making both the upper and lower teeth visible when the mouth is closed, thus creating a "toothy grin". Shape of the nose and jaw: Alligators have wider, shovel-like, U-shaped snouts, while crocodile snouts are typically more pointed or V-shaped. The alligators' broader snouts have been contentiously thought to allow their jaws to withstand the stress of cracking open the shells of turtles and other hard-shelled animals that are widespread in their environments. A 2012 study found very little correlation between bite force and snout shape amongst 23 tested crocodilian species.

query: What's the difference between baking soda and baking powder?
answer:
Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate ($\ce{NaHCO3}$), which produces CO2 only when it gets wet. Baking powder is baking soda plus an acid component, so it produces CO2 both when wet and when heated. The acid in baking powder can be a dry acid like calcium phosphate or tartaric acid.[1][2][3][4]

The key difference is that baking soda requires an acid to react and produce leavening, while baking powder already contains the acid and works on its own. Baking powder also has a double-acting property: it releases CO2 when wet and again when heated.[1][2][3]

query: Does espresso or drip coffee have more caffeine?
answer:
Espresso has more caffeine per unit volume than drip coffee, but a typical serving of espresso contains less total caffeine than a typical serving of drip coffee.

The key distinction is concentration versus total amount. Espresso is a concentrated form of coffee, with about 8 grams of beans per ounce and higher caffeine per milliliter[1][2]. A typical 30 ml serving of espresso contains approximately 65 mg of caffeine[3], while a typical 240 ml serving of drip coffee contains approximately 95 mg[3]. So espresso is stronger per ounce, but because it's served in much smaller volumes, the total caffeine per serving is less than that of drip coffee.

answer: A virus is a non-living infectious agent that replicates inside the host cells of a living organism, while a bacterium is a single-celled prokaryotic organism that can live independently. Antibiotics work by targeting bacterial structures or metabolic pathways—such as cell wall formation and protein synthesis—but they have no effect on viruses because viruses are not alive and do not have these bacterial targets.

query: How do Linux and Windows handle file permissions differently?
answer: Linux and Windows handle file permissions very differently. In Linux, files and directories have read, write, and execution permissions that can be set per user and per group, using commands like `chmod`. In Windows, there are hidden and system attributes, but no equivalent to the executable (x) permission; file permissions are not shared across filesystems. Linux uses dot-prefixing for hidden files, while Windows uses the "hidden" attribute. Linux permissions are tied to the filesystem that created them, whereas Windows has its own permission model.

Martin Luther ( ; ; 10 November 1483 – 18 February 1546) was a German priest, theologian, author, hymnwriter, professor, and former Augustinian friar. Luther was the seminal figure of the Protestant Reformation, and his theological beliefs form the basis of Lutheranism. He is considered one of the most influential figures in Western and Christian history.
Born in Eisleben, Luther was ordained to the priesthood in 1507. He came to reject various teachings and practices of the Roman Catholic Church, in particular the view on indulgences and papal authority. Luther initiated an international debate on these in works like his Ninety-five Theses, which he authored in 1517. In 1520 Pope Leo X demanded that Luther renounce all of his writings, and when Luther refused to do so, excommunicated him in January 1521. Later that year the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, condemned Luther as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms. At the time of Luther's death in 1546, his excommunication was still in effect.

top.text:
There are several common misconceptions about the history of Quechua, as it is frequently identified as the "Inca language". Quechua did not originate with the Incas, had been a lingua franca in multiple areas before the Inca expansions, was diverse before the rise of the Incas, and it was not the native or original language of the Incas. However, the Incas left a linguistic legacy in that they introduced Quechua to many areas where it is still widely spoken today, including Ecuador, southern Bolivia, southern Colombia, and parts of the Amazon basin. The Spanish conquerors continued the official usage of Quechua during the early colonial period and transformed it into a literary language.
The Incas were not known to develop a written form of language; however, they visually recorded narratives through paintings on vases and cups (qirus). These paintings are usually accompanied by geometric patterns known as toqapu, which are also found in textiles. Researchers have speculated that toqapu patterns could have served as a form of written communication (e.g. heraldry or glyphs), however, this remains unclear. The Incas also kept records by using quipus.

top.text:
The Eiffel Tower ( ;  ) is a lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower from 1887 to 1889.
Locally nicknamed "La dame de fer" (French for "Iron Lady") for its use of wrought iron, it was constructed as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair, and to crown the centennial anniversary of the French Revolution. Although initially criticised by some of France's leading artists and intellectuals for its design, it has since become a global cultural icon of France and one of the most recognisable structures in the world. The tower received 5,889,000 visitors in 2022. The Eiffel Tower is the most visited monument with an entrance fee in the world: 6.91 million people ascended it in 2015. It was designated a monument historique in 1964, and was named part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site ("Paris, Banks of the Seine") in 1991.

top.text: The Web was invented by English computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee while working at CERN. He was motivated by the problem of storing, updating, and finding documents and data files in that large and constantly changing organisation, as well as distributing them to collaborators outside CERN. In his design, Berners-Lee dismissed the common tree structure approach, used for instance in the existing CERNDOC documentation system and in the Unix filesystem, as well as approaches that relied on tagging files with keywords, as in the VAX/NOTES system. Instead, he adopted concepts he had put into practice with his private ENQUIRE system (1980), which was built at CERN. When he became aware of Ted Nelson's hypertext model (1965), in which documents can be linked in unconstrained ways through hyperlinks associated with "hot spots" embedded in the text, it helped to confirm the validity of his concept.

top.text: Angkor Wat (; , 'City/Capital of Temples') is a Vaishnava Hindu and Theravada Buddhist temple complex in Siem Reap, Cambodia, and the largest religious complex in the world. Located on a site measuring 162.6 ha within the ancient capital of Angkor, it was constructed between 1113 and 1150 CE during the reign of the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu. From the late 13th century onward, the complex was gradually transformed into a Buddhist temple and has remained an active center of Buddhist worship for centuries. Angkor Wat is noted for its monumental scale, extensive bas-reliefs, and an architectural unity characteristics of Khmer architecture. Unlike most Angkorian temples, it is oriented toward the west. It is a symbol of Cambodia and appears on the Cambodian national flag.

top.text: Beethoven’s hearing loss did not prevent him from composing music, but it made playing at concerts—a lucrative source of income—increasingly difficult. After a failed attempt in 1811 to perform his own Piano Concerto No. 5 (the “Emperor”), which was premiered by his student Carl Czerny, he never performed in public again until he conducted the Ninth Symphony in 1824. A large collection of Beethoven’s hearing aids, such as a special ear horn, can be viewed at the Beethoven House Museum in Bonn, Germany. Despite his obvious distress, Czerny remarked that Beethoven could still hear speech and music normally until 1812. Around 1814 however, by the age of 44, Beethoven was almost totally deaf, and when a group of visitors saw him play a loud arpeggio of thundering bass notes at his piano remarking, “Ist es nicht schön?” (Is it not beautiful?), they felt deep sympathy considering his courage and sense of humor (he lost the ability to hear higher frequencies first). As a result of Beethoven’s hearing loss, his conversation books are an unusually rich written resource. Used primarily in the last ten or so years of his life, his friends wrote in these books so that he could know what they were saying, and he then responded either orally or in the book.

query: Walking 5 km an hour, how long would it take to walk the length of the Great Wall of China?
answer:
At 5 km/h, walking the entire length of the Great Wall would take approximately 4,239 hours, or about 176.6 days of non-stop walking.

The Great Wall is 21,195 km long[1]. At a walking speed of 5 km/h, the time required is 21,195 ÷ 5 = 4,239 hours. Converting to days: 4,239 ÷ 24 ≈ 176.6 days. This is an enormous duration—far longer than any practical walking trip. For comparison, the longest walkable section mentioned in the sources is Badaling at around 7 miles (≈11 km), which would take roughly 2.2 hours at 5 km/h[2]. The Chengdu Little Great Wall is only a few kilometres long[3], and Hadrian's Wall is 135 km long[4].

Note: The sources also mention that the actual walking experience is much slower than 5 km/h due to terrain, elevation changes, and the need to stop for rest and sightseeing.

top.text:
The summit of Everest is the point at which Earth's surface reaches the greatest distance above sea level. Several other mountains are sometimes claimed to be the "tallest mountains on Earth". Mauna Kea in Hawaii is tallest when measured from its base; it rises over 10200 m (33,500 ft) from its base on the mid-ocean floor, but only attains 4205 m (13,800 ft) above sea level.
By the same measure of base to summit, Denali (also called Mount McKinley) in Alaska is taller than Everest as well. Despite its height above sea level of only 6190 m (20,300 ft), Denali sits atop a sloping plain with elevations from 300 to 900 m (980 to 3,000 ft), yielding a height above base in the range of 5300 to 5900 m (17,000 to 19,000 ft); a commonly quoted figure is 5600 m (18,000 ft). By comparison, reasonable base elevations for Everest range from 4200 m (14,000 ft) on the south side to 5200 m (17,000 ft) on the Tibetan Plateau, yielding a height above base in the range of 3650 to 4650 m (12,000 to 15,300 ft).
The summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is 2168 m (7,113 ft) farther from Earth's centre (6384.4 km (3,967 mi)) than that of Everest (6382.3 km (3,966 mi)), because the Earth bulges at the equator. This is despite Chimborazo having a peak of 6268 m (20,560 ft) above sea level versus Mount Everest's 8848 m (29,030 ft).

The best policy is to stick with bottled or purified water[1][2].

answer: If stung by a jellyfish, get out of the water quickly to avoid more stings and drowning. If the sting is serious, seek professional aid as soon as possible. Use vinegar (acetic acid) to rinse the affected area and remove any tentacles, and protect your hands when doing so. After applying vinegar, use gloves or a barrier device to prevent personal injury, then remove any jellyfish parts from the wound. To remove excess sting cells, you may use shaving cream and a safety razor or credit card. Avoid using fresh water to wash the wound.

Although most jellyfish stings are only a painful annoyance, the sting from a box jellyfish or an Irukandji can be fatal, and it is important to take all precautions if stung by a jellyfish. If the sting is serious you should seek professional aid as soon as you can. If not, it is still important to get out of the water quickly to avoid more stings and drowning in the case of a severe allergic reaction to the poison.
A home remedy for the relieving pain/itchiness from a jellyfish sting is to put vinegar on the infected area, except for if the wound is on the eye, where the vinegar can be lightly dabbed around the eye with a cloth but not in the eye. The vinegar will neutralize the venom releasing cells the jellyfish leaves behind. If vinegar is not available you can wash the wound with salt water. Fresh water should not be used to wash the wound. The change in pH can cause additional venom to be released. There is a myth that urine will help the wound. This is untrue and urine will probably end up causing more venom to be released. Many other substances can also aggravate the wound, so it’s important to make sure whatever you use on the sting wound is safe.

query: What are the signs of altitude sickness, and how do I avoid it when hiking in Peru?
answer: Altitude sickness signs include headache, nausea, unusual tiredness, loss of motivation, and dizziness[3]. To avoid it when hiking in Peru, acclimatize for a night or two at a lower altitude (near 2500 m) before going to higher elevations like the Inca Trail[1]. Avoid flying directly into high-altitude cities; instead, take a hot tea or infusion of coca leaves upon arrival[2]. Stay hydrated and rest, as descending is the most effective treatment if symptoms worsen[3].

For malaria, you should take prescription medicine to prevent it, starting multiple days before your trip and continuing during and after.[4]

query: What do I have to keep in mind while camping in the wild?
answer: When camping in the wild, you should keep in mind several key things. First, never camp on private or no-trespassing land, behind fences or gates, as you could be locked in[1]. Second, be aware of potential wildlife, such as rodents and bears, which may be attracted to food waste[2]. Third, prepare for self-sufficiency: you should be ready to cook, find potable water, and manage your own toilet needs[4]. Fourth, consider the risk of crime, dangerous animals, or severe weather depending on your location[5]. Finally, in some regions like Japan, a nojuku tradition supports wild camping, and in Nordic countries, the right to access allows you to pitch your tent almost anywhere away from settlements[4].

query: How do I fix a squeaky door hinge?
answer: To fix a squeaky door hinge, remove the hinge pins up and out from the bottom of each hinge, then unscrew the hinges from both the door and the jamb. After cleaning the hinge, reattach the hinge wings to the door and jamb, and lubricate the pin with a suitable lubricant. For a long-term solution, consider using a proper lubricant like lithium grease or silicone-based lubricants instead of temporary sprays like WD-40. If the hinge is not properly seated in the jamb mortise, you may need to pull the hinge pin, separate the leaves, and set them properly into the mortise.

query: How do I solve a quadratic equation by completing the square?
answer:
To solve a quadratic equation by completing the square, follow these steps:

1. Start with the standard form \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\).
2. Move the constant term \(c\) to the right side of the equation.
3. Divide all terms by \(a\) (the coefficient of \(x^2\)) if \(a \neq 1\).
4. Find \(\left(\frac{1}{2} \cdot b\right)^2\) and add it to both sides of the equation.
5. Factor the left side as a perfect square trinomial: \((x + h)^2 = k\).
6. Take the square root of both sides, then solve the two resulting linear equations.

This method works for any quadratic equation and is especially useful when the coefficient \(a\) is 1 or when the equation does not factor easily.

query: What is surströmming, and why does it smell so bad?
answer: Surströmming is a traditional Swedish food made by fermenting Baltic herring in wooden casks[4]. It smells so bad because of the strong, putrid smell produced during fermentation, which is one of the most putrid food smells in the world[3]. The fermentation process uses just enough salt to prevent the raw herring from rotting while allowing it to ferment[3]. Because of this intense smell, it is often eaten outdoors and is considered bad manners not to invite neighbors before having a surströmmingsskiva[1].

The outbreak started when a woman named Frau Troffea danced on the street, and soon dozens of others joined her. Between 50 and 400 people were affected, dancing for weeks. The phenomenon is believed to have been caused by stress-induced mass hysteria or possibly ergot poisoning.

top.text: Canberra was established following the federation of the Australian colonies to serve as the seat of government for the new nation, being a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, Australia’s two largest cities. The area chosen for the capital had been inhabited by Aboriginal Australians for up to 21,000 years, by groups including the Ngunnawal and Ngambri. European settlement commenced in the first half of the 19th century, evidenced by surviving landmarks such as St John's Anglican Church and Blundells Cottage. On 1 January 1901, federation of the colonies of Australia was achieved. The capital city was founded and formally named as Canberra in 1913. Unusual among Australian cities, it is an entirely planned city, grounded in a design by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin. The Griffins' plan was influenced by the garden city movement and featured geometric motifs aligned with significant topographical landmarks such as Black Mountain, Mount Ainslie, Capital Hill and City Hill. Its design can be viewed from its highest point at the Telstra Tower and the summit of Mount Ainslie. Other notable features include the National Arboretum and Lake Burley Griffin.
